Learning Objectives
List and describe the functions of bone.
Discuss the general anatomy and hierarchical structure of bone.
Describe bone formation and the processes of remodeling and homeostasis.
Explain the biomechanics and composition of bone.
Specify pathologies associated with altered bone morphology and mechanics.
Overview
Functions of bone
Provides mechanical support and protection of vital structures
Regulation of systemic Ca2+ levels
Houses the marrow elements

Types of bones: long, short, flat, and irregular
Formation of bones
Long bones are formed via endochondral ossification, which is the formation of bone from a
cartilage template. Elongation is achieved via a process of columnar organization of
chondrocytes and subsequent hypertrophy.
Flat bones are formed by intramembranous bone formation, which is the formation of bone
via mesenchymal condensates in the absence of a cartilaginous template.
Anatomy
Long bones are composed of three anatomic regions: the diaphysis, metaphysis, and
epiphysis.
Diaphysis: the shaft of a long bone, consisting of a tube of thick cortical bone surrounding a
central canal of trabecular bone, the intramedullary canal
The inner aspect of the cortical bone is called the endosteal surface and is in direct contact
with marrow contents.
The outer region is called the periosteal surface. It is covered by the periosteal membrane,
which is composed of an outer layer of fibrous connective tissue and an inner layer of
undifferentiated, osteogenic progenitor cells. Periosteum also is perforated by vessels and
nerves.
Metaphysis: transition zone from epiphysis to diaphysis; composed of loose trabecular bone
surrounded by cortical bone, which is less thick than the cortical bone of the diaphysis
Epiphysis: specialized end of bone that forms the joint articulation
The epiphyseal plate (physis or physeal scar) divides the epiphysis from the metaphysis and
is synonymous with longitudinal growth of the bone and limb.
The epiphysis is composed of trabecular bone surrounded by a relatively thin layer of
cortical bone.
The articular portion of the bone has a specialized subchondral region underlying the
articular cartilage with cortical morphology.
Flat bones
Flat bones include the pelvis, scapula, skull, and mandible.
The composition of these bones varies from purely cortical to cortical with a thin inner region
of trabecular bone.
Neurovascular anatomy of bone

Innervation—The nerves that innervate bone derive from the periosteum and enter the bone
in tandem with blood vessels. Nerves are found in the haversian canals and the Volkmann
canals.
Sympathetic nerve fibers penetrate the marrow cavity and control the retention and
mobilization of various cell types within bone marrow as a response to trauma.
Blood supply
Nutrient arteries pass through the diaphyseal cortex and enter the intramedullary canal.
These vessels supply blood to the inner two-thirds of the cortical bone and are at risk
during intramedullary reaming.
The outer one-third of the cortical bone derives its blood supply from the periosteal
membrane vessels, which are at risk from periosteal stripping intraoperatively.
Hierarchical Structure of Bone
Macroscopic level
Trabecular bone—Composed of an interconnected network of bony struts (with rod- and
plate-like morphology), which have a maximum thickness of approximately 200 μm and are
approximately 1000 μm in length (Figure 1). Trabecular bone accounts for approximately
20% of total bone mass.
Trabecular bone is porous, with a macroscopic porosity ranging from 30% to 90%.
In osteoporosis, the porosity of trabecular bone is increased because of thinning of
trabecular struts, increased spacing between struts, a reduced number of struts and
alterations in plate versus rod morphology of trabeculae.

Figure 1 Schematic diagram of cortical and trabecular bone shows the different structures
and cell types. 1 = osteoclasts, 2 = osteoblasts, 3 = bone lining cells, 4 = osteocytes, 5 =
marrow space. (Reproduced with permission from Hayes WC: Biomechanics of cortical and
trabecular bone: Implications for assessment of fracture risk, in Mow VC, Hayes WC, eds:
Basic Orthopaedic Biomechanics. New York, NY, Raven Press, 1991, pp 93-142.)
Cortical bone—Dense, compact bone with low porosity and no macroscopic spaces (Figure
2). Cortical bone accounts for approximately 80% of total bone mass.
In the diaphyseal region, cortical bone is load-bearing. Osteons and haversian canals are
oriented along the primary axis of the bone.
In the metaphysis and epiphysis, cortical bone serves as a border to trabecular bone. It
supports only a portion of the load, which is primarily carried by the trabecular bone in
these regions.
Cortical bone in the metaphyseal and epiphyseal region frequently serves as soft-tissue
attachment sites for tendons and ligaments.

Microscopic level
Woven bone is primary bone characterized by a random orientation of collagen and
mineral.
Lamellar bone is secondary bone that results from the remodeling of woven bone into an
organized bone tissue.
Lacunae are ellipsoidal spaces in bone occupied by osteocytes. Small channels through the
bone called canaliculi connect the lacunae and contain osteocyte cell processes that
interact with other cells. Fluid flows through the canalicular channels during loading and is
thought to be a mechanism through which mechanical strains are imparted to osteocytes.
Figure 2 Diagram of the structure of cortical bone shows the types of cortical lamellar bone: the
internal circumferential system, interstitial system, osteonal lamellae, and outer circumferential
system. The diagram also shows the intraosseous vascular system that serves the osteocytes and
connects the periosteal and medullary blood vessels. The haversian canals run primarily

longitudinally through the cortex, whereas the Volkmann canals create oblique connections
between the haversian canals. Cement lines separate each osteon from the surrounding bone.
Periosteum covers the external surface of the bone and consists of two layers: an osteogenic
(inner) cellular layer and a fibrous (outer) layer. (Adapted from Miller JD, McCreadie BR, Alford AI,
et al: Form and function of bone, in Einhorn TA, O’Keefe RJ, Buckwalter JA, eds: Orthopaedic Basic
Science: Foundations of Clinical Practice, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2007, pp 129-159.)
Extracellular Matrix
Composition of the extracellular matrix (ECM) is 60% to 70% inorganic (mineral) and 20% to
25% organic components. From an engineering perspective, bone can be thought of as a
nanocomposite material consisting of an organic (collagen) matrix reinforced with a
discontinuous inorganic (mineral) phase.
Organic matrix is 90% type I collagen; 5% other collagen types (III and IV), non-collagenous
proteins, and growth factors; and the remaining tissue volume is occupied by water.
Collagen
Type I collagen is the primary ECM component of bone tissue.
Type I collagen is fibril-forming, with a triple helical structure (three alpha chains) that
contributes tensile strength to the ECM.
Fibrils are intrinsically stable because of noncovalent interconnections and covalent cross-
links between lysine residues.
Mineral component (reinforces the collagen matrix)
Composed primarily of calcium and phosphate (with some substitution of sodium,
magnesium, and carbonate) in the form of hydroxyapatite and tricalcium phosphate
Tropocollagen helices in the fibrils are organized in a quarter-staggered arrangement, with
empty regions (hole zones) between the ends and pores running lengthwise between
collagen fibrils.
Hydroxyapatite crystal nucleation and growth in these hole zones is thermodynamically
favorable.
Helps to regulate systemic mineral homeostasis by acting as a reservoir for inorganic ions,
including Ca2+, PO4– and Mg2+
Emerging evidence suggests that bone also aids in the regulation of systemic glucose
metabolism. In addition to well-established insulin-signaling that proves critical for bone

anabolism, the expression of osteocalcin and lipocalin-2 have been demonstrated to be
closely linked with systemic energetics and metabolism.1,2
Non-collagenous ECM proteins in bone
Vitamin K–dependent proteins: osteocalcin, periostin, matrix gla-protein
Small integrin-binding ligand N-linked glycoproteins: osteopontin, bone sialoprotein, dentin
matrix protein-1, dentin sialophosphoprotein, matrix extracellular phopsphoglycoprotein
RGD-containing proteins: adhesive proteins containing the arginine-glycine-aspartate motif;
fibronectin, fibrillin 1, fibrillin 2, perlecan, thrombospondins
Phosphoproteins: phosphorylated (negatively charged) extracellular proteins; interact with
calcium; thought to play a role in mineralization
Growth factors and cytokines: bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), BMP antagonists
(Noggin, Chordin), insulin-like growth factors (IGF-1, IGF-2, and IGF-binding proteins),
transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-ß) and TGF-ß-binding proteins, fibroblastic growth
factors, Dickkopf proteins
Proteoglycans: macromolecules composed of protein core and glycosaminoglycan side
chains; biglycan, decorin, fibromodulin, perlecan, osteoglycin (mimecan), osteoadherin.
Extracellular enzymes: lysyl oxidase, alkaline phosphatase, matrix metalloproteinases,
phosphate-regulating neutral endopeptidase, X-linked
Bone Cells
Bone is one of the only tissues that possesses specialized, predominantly resident cells that
are charged with anabolic (osteoblasts) and catabolic (osteoclasts) functions. In addition to the
osteocytes, these three cell types are primarily responsible for many of the classic functions of
bone and bone remodeling. However, a number of cells within bones, including endothelial
cells and pericytes associated with bone vasculature, and various cells within the marrow
compartment are of hematopoietic or mesenchymal lineage.
Osteoblasts: bone-forming cells found at an active mineralizing surface
Phenotypic markers of osteoblasts include alkaline phosphatase; osteocalcin; osteonectin;
osteopontin; and phosphate-regulating neutral endopeptidase, X-linked. Osteoblasts also
express parathyroid hormone (PTH) receptor and actively secrete type I collagen.
Osteoblasts arise from mesenchymal marrow stromal cells and periosteal membrane cells.
A series of cellular regulators serve as differentiation cues for osteoblast development from
stem cell to mature osteoblast/osteocyte.

Runt-related transcription factor 2 and Osterix are essential transcription factors required
for osteoblastic commitment.
The mature osteoblast has a lifespan of 100 days. It can then become a bone-lining cell or
an osteocyte, or it can undergo apoptosis. Bone-lining cells are relatively inactive cells that
cover the surfaces of bone, which may become activated at a later time.
Osteoblast differentiation is regulated by several cytokines, including BMPs, Indian and
sonic hedgehog proteins, PTH, TGF-ß superfamily members, and Wnts.
Osteocytes: mature osteoblasts encased in the mineralized matrix of bone
Osteocytes reside in the lacunar spaces of trabecular and cortical bone. They are
nonmitotic and are not highly synthetic but should not be considered quiescent.
Osteocytes have numerous cell processes that communicate with other cells via the
canaliculi.
Signaling between neighboring osteocytes is mediated by gap junctions, and TGF-ß1 plays
an integral role in facilitating the formation of these gap junctions.3 The gap junctions that
occur at the end of osteocyte dendritic processes are important for sensing of the
mechanical environment within bone tissue.
Osteocytes are metabolically active, load-sensing cells, secrete receptor activator of nuclear
factor-? B ligand (RANKL), and regulate adult bone remodeling directly.
Osteocytes regulate bone-forming osteoblasts by secreting sclerostin (SOST), a product of
the SOST gene. SOST inhibits Wnt signaling by binding to the co-receptors lipoprotein
receptor-related protein 5/6 and antagonize downstream signaling in osteoblasts.
Osteoclasts: bone-resorbing cells of a hematopoietic lineage, directly differentiated from
monocytes
Marker proteins include tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase, calcitonin receptor, receptor
activator of nuclear factor-? B (RANK), and cathepsin K.
Osteoclasts are from a hematopoietic lineage and differentiate directly from a monocytic
precursor. Multinuclear osteoclast polykaryons form via fusion of mononuclear precursors,
a process that requires RANKL and macrophage-colony stimulating factor.
Mature osteoclasts attach to bone surfaces and form a sealing zone (ruffled border).
Osteoclasts secrete cathepsin K, collagenase, hydrogen ions, and other hydrolytic enzymes
in the sealed zone. Mineral is first dissolved by the secreted acidic products, and the
organic matrix is subsequently degraded via the secretion of enzymes (collagenase,
gelatinase).

Differentiation and activity of osteoclasts are regulated primarily by RANKL and
osteoprotegerin (OPG, or tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 11B). RANKL
binds to its cognate receptor, RANK, on the membrane of monocyte/macrophage. OPG is a
decoy receptor, that binds to and sequesters RANKL, preventing its interaction with RANK
and subsequently inhibiting osteoclast activity.
Bone Homeostasis and Remodeling
Bone remodeling
Bone is a dynamic tissue that constantly undergoes remodeling via coupled osteoblastic
bone formation and osteoclastic bone resorption. Although remodeling is most closely
associated with a response to mechanical loading, a number of pathologic states may result
in decoupled osteoblast-osteoclast functions, leading to focal or diffuse alterations in bone
composition, morphology, and properties.
The regulatory mechanisms of remodeling are critical to understanding bone homeostasis
and bone metabolic disease states. Our primary understanding of remodeling focuses on the
RANK-RANKL-OPG system that substantially contributes to osteoblast-osteoclast coupling;
however, numerous other signaling pathways also play important roles.
Bone mass turns over completely every 4 to 20 years, depending on age, activity, and
metabolic states. In adulthood, the mean rate of turnover is approximately 5% of total mass
per year.
Trabecular bone remodeling
Osteoclast-mediated resorption of trabeculae results in the development of a resorption pit
called a Howship lacuna.
Local osteoblasts are subsequently recruited by the degraded collagen within the resorption
pits because osteoblasts have been shown to possess an endyctic collagen receptor,
uPARAP/Endo180.4
Cortical bone remodeling
Osteoclasts tunnel through bone to form a cutting cone of resorption.
Blood vessel formation occurs in the cutting cone.
Osteoblast recruitment and new bone formation occur in the resorbed space of the cutting
cone.
New bone is formed around the new vessel and the resulting structure is called an osteon.
The haversian canal refers to the encased vessel space, which is oriented along the major
axis of the bone.

Mechanisms of osteoblast/osteoclast coupling
The biologic activity of osteoblasts is closely associated with that of osteoclasts; intercellular
signaling mechanisms are being studied.
Osteoblastic regulation of osteoclast function has been well documented. PTH is a pro-
osteoclastogenic cytokine that acts via osteoblast cell-surface receptors. These receptors
stimulate the synthesis of factors, including RANKL and macrophage-colony stimulating
factor, critical to osteoclast development.
In addition to secreting pro-osteoclastogenic RANKL, osteoblasts also can produce OPG,
which functions as a decoy molecule for the RANK receptor and prevents RANK-RANKL
coupling. Therefore, osteoblasts have positive and negative regulatory effects on osteoclast
activity.
Osteoclast activity also is regulated by systemic factors, such as serum calcium levels and
circulating hormones.
Vitamin D and PTH stimulate osteoclastic activity.
Calcitonin reduces osteoclastic activity.
Osteoclast regulation of osteoblast differentiation and activity is less understood. One
hypothesis is that osteoclastic bone resorption releases bioactive factors (BMP, TGF-ß, IGF-1)
that stimulate osteoblast differentiation and new bone formation.
Biomechanics of Bone
Elastic deformation: classical, Hookean behavior in which a material will return to its original
shape and dimensions if an applied load is released
Plastic deformation: permanent deformation of a material as a function of an applied load 
Viscoelastic behavior: time-dependent mechanical behavior, frequently described by
properties such as stress relaxation and creep 
Stress relaxation: an observed decrease in stress in response to mechanical strain 
Creep: a constant state of stress despite an increase in material strain 
Fatigue—The behavior of a tissue or material in response to cyclic loading over time. Fatigue
behavior can be defined in terms of the number of loading cycles, magnitude of the applied
cyclic loads, and frequency of applied loads. In bone, fatigue behavior is closely related to the
existence and development of microcracks, which can propagate through the tissue matrix.
Fracture toughness—The resistance of a material to the propagation of a crack in a specific
mode of loading. The critical crack length that will induce failure in uniaxial tension (KIC),
calculated by the formula:

the case of KIC), s is the applied stress, and a is the critical crack length.
Strain: the change in a dimension of a specimen over the original dimension of the specimen
Stress: an applied external load divided by the cross-sectional area of a specimen
Modulus of elasticity: a material property often used interchangeably with stiffness, but only
applicable at a material level rather than construct level; defined as the slope of the linear
region of a stress-strain curve

Biomechanics of Bone
The biomechanical behavior of bone is not dissimilar from engineering materials, aside
from the ability of living bone to repair and remodel over time. Therefore, many of the
terms used to describe the mechanical behavior of engineering materials are applicable
to bone tissue.5
Compositional Basis for Bone Mechanics
Collagen—Type I collagen plays an immeasurable role in the mechanics of bone, and most
attribute the ductile behavior of bone to this organic matrix. Perhaps nearly as important to
the periodic structure of collagen fibrils is the manner in which the fibrils interact with each
other via cross-linking. Pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline facilitate trivalent cross-links in type
I collagen and may aid in energy dissipation during loading, thereby imparting a toughening
mechanism to bone tissue.
Hydroxyapatite—Bone mineral is integral to the mechanical behavior of bone tissue. Bone
mineral is crystalline in nature; however, aspects of the crystal structure, dispersion within the
collagen matrix, and purity (substitution with carbonate, for instance) play an important role in
the mechanical behavior of bone. Lower remodeling rates lead to enhanced crystallinity, which
generally is associated with more brittle bone mechanics.
Water—Water within bone tissue may be bound to the organic matrix or to bone mineral. The
association of water with collagen is important for the toughness (energy absorption) of bone
tissue, and the amount of this collagen-bound water decreases with patient age.

Pathology Associated With Altered Bone Morphology and
Biomechanics
Aging—Beginning in the fourth decade of life, 2% to 5% of endosteal cortical bone and 5% to
10% of cancellous bone is lost. This leads to a substantial reduction in static (tensile,
compressive, elastic modulus) and dynamic (fatigue, fracture toughness) properties of bone
(Figure 3).
Sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease—Autosomal recessive disorder resulting in increased
bone mass from decreased SOST production. SOST is a BMP antagonist and Wnt inhibitory
glycoprotein primarily expressed by osteocytes, which has a negative effect on osteoblast-
mediated bone formation. Aberrant SOST production leads to a pro-anabolic environment,
resulting in sclerosis of bone.6 SOST-deficient rodent models demonstrate that a loss of this
Wnt inhibition results in a lack of mechanoadaptation in bone despite an overall increase in
bone mass.7
Osteogenesis imperfecta—A family of 19 genetic disorders that appear to primarily affect
bone; often referred to as brittle bone disease. In addition to bony changes, other common
features include a blue-tinged sclera, respiratory disorders, hearing loss, short stature, and
dental complications. Most nonlethal osteogenesis imperfecta involves mutations in COL1A1
and COL1A2 genes that lead to alterations in the collagen matrix and the mineral component
of bone. In general, osteogenesis imperfecta results in thin collagen fibers and
hypermineralization, causing an inability to absorb energy from external loading and
culminating in brittle failure.8
Diabetes mellitus—Accumulation of advanced glycation end products is associated with
hypermineralization and a loss of mechanical performance in trabecular bone in type 1 and
type 2 diabetes mellitus. The relationship between the accumulation of advanced glycation
end products and hypermineralization appears to be related to a reduced rate of bone
remodeling, at least in type 2 diabetes mellitus. This leads to the clinical/epidemiologic
observation of an increased rate of fragility fractures in patients with diabetes mellitus.9
Postmenopausal osteoporosis—Perhaps one of the most well-studied conditions that affects
the material and structural properties of bone, postmenopausal osteoporosis continues to
evoke new therapeutic and diagnostic strategies for endocrinologists and orthopaedists. A
reduction in systemic estrogen associated with menopause leads to osteoblast/osteoclast
decoupling, favoring osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Radiographically, this decoupling

leads to reduced bone mass that, on the micro scale, is associated with decreased trabecular
thickness, decreased trabecular number, and reduced bone mineral content.
Figure 3 Graph shows the trade-off between strength and toughness. In many materials, ductility
or toughness is sacrificed for high stiffness and strength (and vice versa). Bone has a somewhat
unique ability to balance these two competing properties. This balance can be compromised in
disease in which the tissue becomes overly stiff at the expense of the ability to dissipate energy
and is brittle. Alternatively, some diseases have a negative effect on stiffness and strength and
deform a great deal under relatively low load levels, leading to bone deformity. (Reproduced from
Burr DB, Wallace JM: Bone biomechanics, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations
of Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp
133-142.)
